All your Relations here in ye Country are now, I thank God, very well: my humble Service to Mr Principal & all other my good Friends. The Lord bless you & direct you in all your undertakings. I am

note.value: 488. SIR JOHN LOWTHER OF SOCKBRIDGE TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
I have yrs of ye 29th of June recom~ending my Cousen yr Son to
ye church of Distington & sld be very glad to serve him either by my self or others, accordingly have been his solicitor to my Ld Comr Rawlinson who seems not to doubt but in some time to provide for him; as to this Pticular desir'd I shal make you judge of wt I am to doe therin; you know ye School of St Bees is very meanly p~vided of all helps but a Mastr, my design has been so to annex that Living to ye School, yt ye Mastr being therby wel p~vided for, ye Revenue he now has or ye greatest part wch does not p~perly belong to him, might be apply'd for ye support of Ushers, Writing Mastrs & Accomptts &c. or if any other p~vision cld be made for ye School, yt then this Living sld be supply'd by some p~son like to Flamsteed, Mr Rook or one well skill'd in Mathamaticks who might be of use to ye Town of Whitehaven, according to ye instance of Mr Norwood who by inhabiting a few years at Bermudas, rais'd yt place from a very low condition to be ye best Navigators of ye World. I am thus p~ticuler in excuse for any hesitation I can make in concurring with yr
desires, but doubt not one way or other I may serve yr Son, wch shal be ye endeavour of
For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydall Westmrland

note.value: 491. ROGER FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
I ye unworthyest of your sons doth once more presume upon your love and kindness (wch hath been more alredy then I shall ere be able to requite) towards me, feareing now least my monie should not answer my expectation, haveing disbursed more alredy, then I expected to have done, this great many weeks, espetially to ye scriviner
(who is with us now) and ye necessarys adjoyning their too, hath allmost run me aground. is ye cause of my praesuming boldness in requesting so unreasonable a kindness from you, but being very sencible yt you have been (all along) more kind to me then I have disarved, makes me ashamed allmost to prosecute any further in desireing you, yet hoping you will grant my request, and procure me some monie as soon as you can conveniently, and in so doing you will much oblidge him who makes it his dayly study (through Gods assistance) to requite, and become ye dutifulest of your Sons
ffor Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal these Leave this at Mr Brownsword's Shop in Kendal

note.value: 494. GEORGE FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
I have received yours of the last month, and am not in the least concerned at this disappointment, forasmuch as it's but what they must dayly expect who have to doe in such things, all Sr that I have to say, is that I hope your other friends will be more kind to you and not fall short of what may be reasonably expected from them: I have met with another disappointment, and that is my design at Lincoln Coll: for I was there tould by the Master that unless I was borne in Yorkshire, or in Bop: of Lincoln I could in nowise stand; and he added that my being related to Bp: Fleming the Founder would do me no good, forasmuch as he died before the Statutes were made; and one
Rotheram being intrusted with the composing of them granted the greatest priviledge to those of the town of Rotheram; he expressed a great kindness for me, & was very glad to see the Pedegree of their Founder, of which I let him take a Coppy; haveing now Sr miss'd in this I must wholy relie upon you for the future, for some preferment; and I do not question but you can judge how ardent I am upon it; for which to make myself capable I have addicted my self wholy to the study of Divinity & the Fundamentals thereof; following the advise of the Bp. of Sarum in his Pastoral; which I hope will do more for me then that excellent method Dr Mill, as he writ to you, had put me in; for that fine method of his was nothing, but that I should read Josephus & the Septuagint, but we must give great men liberty to talk great though they do but little; Sr I should be glad of anything until better may be had, which how shortly however it may be, I shall I fear esteme it long. I am much obliged to my most kind sister Alice for writing
in my behalfe unto Ms Smith, to whom Sr I desire you to give my Servise & to all my Brothers, & be pleased to grant your Blessing to
Sr my leg is almost well, being no wise troublesome to me.
For Sr Daniel Fleming att Rydal near Kendal Westmoreland These.

note.value: 496. ROGER FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
Yours I have received and am very sensible that it's your mind and desire yt I should do well, and withdraw my inclinations from those worldly, and momentary pleasures, and redeem my time, which I thank God for, I may saffely say my coorse of life I have much altered (I hope to ye better) and those pleasures which formerly tempted me to injustice, are become odious in my sight, though this childish falling out which hath been betwix my Master and me, may make you apt to think my former lines a fable, and I am more conscious of it since I have deferred giveing you an account of it so long, but hopeing yt it would not have comed to your ear, made me refrain writeing, as much for ye Masters credit, as to my own reputation, knowing myself free of it,
which was very apparent to all about us, and made them admire to see a man so insensed for a thing of naught, but I am apt to think yt ye old grudge is not cold, and againe finding me more submissive then formerly makes him more severar then usuall he hath been, but I am resolved to endure whatever come with patience till Chrismas, if it be your pleasure to let me continue so long this is all desireing you to take no notice of it, but let me have ye burding and I shall undergoe it cherefully haveing this in my mind, yt whosoever is without troubles in this world hath his share of them in ye world to come and in so doing you much oblidge him who makes it his daily study to become ye dutifulest of your sons
For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal These

note.value: 497. GEORGE FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
Now at length I hope I shall have the opportunity of shewing my selfe an obediant Son, in corresponding with your commands even in that to which I must confess my selfe to have had alwayes a natural avertion; for Ember Week is now at hand, and so an Ordenation will be very shortly, in order for which I have been a long time now moking preparation; Dr Mill hath been pleased to give me a title, so that I want now nothing but to be examined by the Bishops Chaplain, of all which in my next I will give you an exact account. Sr I have now sent you this Quarters accounts, that you may be better able to know what I shall want in the next; in which besidse those things which occur every Quarter, I am obliged to determine which it selfe will not come much short of 10 pounds, & all this charge I shall be att before Tom come at Lent; besides which I must have what is fitting for one in Orders,
as a Gown, a Cassok, and a Hatt, without which I shall not be able to appear in the Country about Oxford, nor can exercise my selfe in preaching as I resolved to doe; it will also requesite for me know Hebrew. Sr we have not any new think of late printed; its said Woods Athenae Ox: will be answered. Dr Mills G: Testament is now finished all but the Prolegomena. Gloster Hall is now reedifiing, and Dr Woodruf of C: Ch: is to be the Governor of it, and it will be endowed. Sr I desire you will be pleased to give my Servise to all my brothers & Sisters, and to grant your blessing to Sr
Sr I had forgot to mention the charges of Ordenation. For Sr Daniel Fleming att Rydal near Kendal Westmoreland Theses.

note.value: 501. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO GEORGE FLEMING.

text.p:
Yours of the 9th instant I have received, which was so farr from my expectation as it hath given me no little trouble. I was in great hopes that my last Letter unto you, might have deserved a better Return. When Sons pretend In~ate Aversions (& I cannot tell what) against
their own Good, & their Fathers desires; it often happens that such sons may live to repent it, & see ye vanity of their own fond wandering Projects & Designes. You have been a long time in building up (to my great charge) a fair Reputation, & to make you fit for Preferment; and one indiscreet Action will make all Totter that you have done, in case you act not very prudently for the Future. Parents are obliged to assist their children, as well as they reasonably may, so long as they act well according to their directions; But when as children will do ill, otherwise than their Parents would have them, & will also turn Projectors, and act apparently to their own Prejudice; then Parents are not under any obligation to assist them in their own fond and expensive Fancies. And in case of their suffering thereby, they can justly blame not any but themselves. Persons who are neither Dunces nor Debouchees, I see no reason that the Caprich of a Chaplain should debarr them (who are well affected to the King & Church) from Preferment; and I can name several who have been denyed Orders by one Bishop, and have been ordained Deacon & Priest by another. It is very difficult to get a good place in ye Fleet or Army; and I do not at all think you fit for either of them. It is more difficult to procure you a good place at court; and it is not every one there that will prove a Sr Joseph Williamson. Your brother William is now in London, and you may consult him (with Sr Jo. Lowther, Sr Christo. Musgrave, & Sr Geo. Fletcher), who hath more Acquaintances there then I have. Your most worthy Principal (to whom I have written by this Post) hath been alwayes very obligeing towards you, & I would have you advise well with him in this your weighty affair. I know young men have often a great longing to see London, & if it be so with you, then perhaps a week or a Fourthnights stay
there may do you good, and shew you ye vanity of your designes. If you have a mind to come hither this winter, I shall be glad to see you, that we may consider together what may best be done. If you leave Oxford, I think you had best take an exact Catalogue of all your Bookes, Goods, & Chattells, & not to sell any of them, But to leave them with my Cosin (& Godson) Henry Browham, who I doubt not will take care of them during your Absence. In case you shall think fit to come hither, you may buy a little Horse (of 40 or 50 Shillings) that will bring you down, takeing short journeyes, or you may hire an Horse from London of ye Kendal Carrier, if you shall be there. The Lord direct you in all your wayes and Actions; and be not like to those persons, who grow Elder & Fonder. Remember me to all my Friends. I have received ye Bookes according to your Letter. I am
In case you shall come hither, you may hire an Horse as you did ye last time, if you can.

note.value: 503. REV. POSTHUMUS WHARTON TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
Your Sonn's diligence was the condition I made in my last Letter to you; and if they had used the same diligence before, that they have done of late, they had (I doubt not) been at this time in that forwardness which I then mention'd, but their former remissness makes it necessary for me to begg their company a small time longer, which I hope will be to their advantage, which is the sole end I aim at, your son Roger is much reform'd which hath been a great satisfaction to me, I begg you'l please to lay your commands upon them to be carefull of their business in this vacation; and not to squander their time, and if they continue their diligence till Easter, I hope they will have conquer'd much of the difficulty - If you have any thoughts (Sr) to send them to St. John's Coll: in Camb. (where I made bold to tell you, yt I doubted not but they might obtain the priviledges belonging to the school) I beg you'l please to give me some intimation of it that I may write to their Tutour to provide them a fit chamber &c
Sr John Otway and his Lady are expected at Ingmire every day I am
Honoured Sr Your most obliged ffaithfull Servt
This ffor the Worshipful Sr Daniel ffleming at Rydal

note.value: 505. REV. POSTHUMUS WHARTON TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
I am sollicited to give you this trouble, though I know it superfluous, being well assured that you will shew what favour to Sedbergh Justice will allow, and to request more were a crime soe bold as I would not willingly incurr - The Inhabitants of Burton (Sr) intend (I am inform'd) to bring a suit against the Parish of Sedbergh; for
charges in Thom: Cartmels case, but your letter to Mr Heblethwait gives us good incouragement, that wee shall not have that added to the burthen we must sustain in providing for him and his children; who was (it seems) but a very small time a servant among us, and that, 5 or 6 years agoe; I have look'd for your sonns (Sr) these 3 or 4 days, and am very desirous to receive them, that I may doe you in them what service I am able, and what I acknowledge due, from
Honoured Sr Your Worship's most ffaithfull humble Servt
This ffor the Worshipfull Sr Daniel ffleming Kt att Kendale

note.value: 508. GEORGE FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
I have even now received yours, & deliver'd the enclosed to Dr Mill, according to the directions. My cosin Browhams are now both at London, & have been there this week. so that I cannot give you any other account of Queens, then that it is very full, espetially the Foundation, upon which it will be very difficult to gett my B: Roger a Chamber. I could have wished him here a week since, for then he would have avoided the fiers, which the foundation-men are so affraid of. Sr I am not able to express the high sence I have of this your most unparallel'd kindness in granting my humble petition, petition I say, for I never had it in my mind, or if I should have had, ever durst I have pretended to have made a demand of it; which I conceive must have been so, before that Dr Mill could with any reason have
branded me with a disobedience, then which there is not any think I more detest, & abhor, of which my whole life shall be a demonstration. It was Sr upon the Drs account that I defer'd my last letter so long, he being pleased to promise to excuse me to you in his for it, yet I cannot find it so, but rather the contrary. Sr I a very unwilling to come into the North at this time, because the journey is long, and the North being not a place to procure preferment in, it will consequently beget another; & with all my long distance from London may cause a disappointment, but Sr my going to London may greatly facilitate any business, and keep those friends which are in town mindfull of me, to be upon the spot to solicit, is the shurest way to acquire what wee desire, & this I take to be the best time, forasmuch as ye king is now in Eng: the Parl: sitting, & so those there which will perhaps in a very short time be in the Country: if Sr upon this you think it fitting for me to go to London, I shall take care to live so, as one who goes not to spend, but to gett money; & shall send you an account of all my Books & other things, of wch what you like Tom may bring you, & I hauing a few, Roger may take all the rest; the Bedding, Chairs, & table &c may be of great use to him. Sr this Quarter will be up about the midle of this moneth, & if I enter upon the next Quarter I must pay for it although I leave Oxford, & so Sr I desire your pleasure in it & rest
Sr to hire a horse here in Oxon~ at this time of ye year, would be dearer than to buy one.

Sr to leave Oxon~, I suppose it will be very needless & chargeable for me to determine, & therefore it will be best for me to
leave Oxon~ before I shall be sum~oned to it; which will be about the week before Shrovetide; but in this as you please. For Sr Daniel Fleming att Rydal near Kendal in Westmoreland These.

note.value: 510. REV. HENRY BROUGHAM TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
My Cousin George acquainted me some few daies agoe that you intended a Second Son for ye ffoundation at Queens. It is not to be
doubted but he will find all due encouragement from those in whose power it is to befriend him; and for my own part, I must look upon my self peculiarly obliged to serve him wth all the kindness I can shew him, or interest I can make. Indeed I must own that I have been very in different as to ye business of pupilling since I return'd from Buckden, there being then other establisht Tutours very fit and able to serve ye Colledge: and the Late Bishop of Lincolne having been pleased to add an augmentation to my ffellowship, it has made me ye Willinger to leave those advantages to others wch accrue from pupills. However if you send up yr Son, I will either undertake the care & tuition of him myself, or place him where I will take effectual care he shall not be neglected, wch of these two you are most desirous of: And please to doe me ye justice to believe I can never think any thing a trouble whereby I may answer the obligations I have to be serviceable to you or yours.

Sr Cousin Harry being so lately acquainted wth ye customs & constitutions of ye Colledge, he will give what directions are necessary about ye Sending up his Brother. Pray give my Service & respects to him & all belonging to Rydal, and please to let him know, that Mr Penny
of Hampton Powel is dead, and 'tis believed Mr Addison will accept ye place; ye reason of wch he can possibly divine. I am
Hond Sr Yr Obedient Son & Servant
To The Right Worshipfull Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal Westmrland This.

note.value: 514. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO REV. HENRY BROUGHAM.

text.p:
Haveing writ in January last unto my Son George, that I designed to send unto Oxford his Brother Roger by Tho. Burnyates, and that I intended my Son Roger should be entered in Queens College as a Battelar; and if you would take him for your Pupil, that I would recommend him unto your care: my son George acquaints me in his last Letter, that you are willing to be Roger's Tutor, and to take charge of him. I have writ unto Mr Provost concerning ye same, wishing that you may be my Sons Tutor, in case Mr Provost shall approve thereof, which I hope he will do. I have writ unto my Son George, acquainting him with what money I have sent by Tho. Burnyates, and how ye same shall be disposed of, and I doubt not George will consult you, and be advised by you in this, & his other affairs. I question not your care of, and kindness to my Son; & I am very hopeful that He will be very civil, studious, & obedient. What
supplies he shall from time to time stand need of, shall be carefully sent you by

note.value: 518. ROGER FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p: With no small trouble, do I write now unto you, haveing found things at my arrival quite contrary to my expectation; being the other day before my Cosin Browham, and Mr Waffe, who frely declared unto me their minds, wishing me both well (as fare as I could perceive) told me that they were both very unwilling yt I should enter upon ye foundation, feareing yt I should not onely indure ye slavery very unwillingly, but yt I should be scharse able to performe ye exercise of ye house, it being so strictly lookt for, from ye foundation men, at ye hearing of which I was not a little surprized with admiration, but being very unwiling to enter upon any other, then what you had resolved of, before I heard from you, I desired my Cosin Browham to write, at which he promised he would, and give you a full account what he thought best to be done. Now I desire you to be as kind as you possible can, and if you'l be pleased to advance me a little, I shall use all ye endeavours I can, to answer your expectation, and cost you as little as may be. So I rest your dutyful

My Cosin Lauther hath been very kind to me since I came. I have here sent you a Bill of what I disbursed in ye rode. Pray return my sister many thanks for me My sister Wilson gave me five shillings, Allso my sister Alice, and my Brother Tatham gave me either of them five shillings, and my sister Bouch two and six pence.

note.value: 521. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO REV. HENRY BROUGHAM.

text.p: I received yours by Tho. Burnyate, and my son George (haveing made some stay in visiting his Sister) is lately arrived here & acquaints me how much I am obliged to you concerning my son Roger. I return you many thankes for your kind Letter, & for your Frank dealing with me therein. He haveing acquainted me, how long he had been ye Head-Schollar in Sedbergh School, with what Bookes he had read there, & with what Exercise he dayly made; I did (without any other particular examination) take it for granted that he was a competent Schollar; But since you acquaint me otherwise, I hope he may continue a Battelar amongst you, until he shall be fit for better Preferment, or at least until I shall otherwise dispose of him. Whilst you shall think fit to continue his Tutor, I doubt not you'l encourage him to Redeem as much of ye time he hath lost as he can possibly dureing the time he shall remain in Oxford; & I hope in case you shall turne my son over to another Tutor, that then he will do ye like. Let me know what supplyes my son Roger shall stand need of a little before Tho: Burnyate shall begin his journey, that I may send them by him. My humble service to Mr Provost, & all other good Friends with you. I am, Sr
Your most obliged & affectionate Kinsman & God-Father

note.value: 522. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO ROGER FLEMING.

text.p:
Haveing received a Letter from my Cosin Henry Brougham, & another from your selfe by Tho. Burnyate; I am sorry to hear that things do not answer either your, or my Expectation. It seems you are not so good a Schollar, as one might reasonably expect from one that had been so long ye Head-schollar in Sedbergh school, that had read so many Latine & Greek Authors there, & that had made dayly so much Exercise. Herein it seems you have both couzen'd yourselfe & me, which will render it very difficult (I fear) for you to get any Preferment in ye College, unless you shall redeem your lost time, by being very studious, civil, & industrious. It will not be for your credit, to take you soon from Oxford: therefore I would not have you discouraged in getting what University learning you can possibly. Who knows but that your Religious, Studious & Civil Deportment may help you in time to some preferment; & to that end I would have you to continue a Battelar for some time, which will give you opportunity enough of encreasing your Learning & Knowledge. I have writ unto my cosin Brougham, who I doubt not will direct & advise you for ye best, whilst he shall continue your Tutor; & when as he shall turn you over unto another, I hope such Tutor will do ye like. Be careful that you do not squander away your time, haveing lost too much thereof already. Be not weary of well doing; but rather be dayly more & more diligent. Difficult things may most of them be overcome by patience and Industry. Your brother William intends to come home by ye way of Bath. Your brother Michael and his men are gone
for Flanders. Give my thanks to all who shew you any kindness, & so long as you continue studious, civil & a good husband, you shall be reasonably supplyed. The Lord bless you, I am

note.value: 523. REV. POSTHUMUS WHARTON TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p: Your Son James (as I made bold to inform you) would really learn very well if he would confine his thoughts to his study only, but I am told by those to whom he imparts his mind, that his Inclinations are too bent upon military affairs, which I doubt will very much impede his progress in Learning, if they be not diverted, I have told him my thoughts in the matter as fully as I can, and must now submitt the further management of it to your own great prudence, but shall always (as I am confess'dly bound) be ready to serve you to the utmost of my power, whom am
Honoured Sr Your most obliged humble Servt
This ffor the worshipfull Sr Daniel ffleming Kt att Rydal

note.value: 524. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO ROGER FLEMING.

text.p:
I writ to my Cosin Henry Brougham, & to you, ye 28th of April last; but hearing not any thing from either of you, I am affraid that my Letters are miscarried; therefore I have here inclosed sent you
a copy of them. Soon after this shall come unto your hand, let me hear from you by ye Post, & let me know whether you have received my former Letters, & how you like Oxford. I shall be very glad to hear of your Health & well doing. Your brother William is lately come home from London, by ye way of Bath: I have yet heard not any thing from my Son Michael since his going beyond sea. All your Relations in ye Country are well. The Lord bless you. My service to your Tutor & all other good Friends.

note.value: 525. ROGER FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
The letters which you sent to my Cosin Brougham, and me, we received several weeks agoe, and was purposed to have write ere this, but calling to mind yt Tom: was to come a little after Whitsuntide, he though it might do as well, to defer writeing a little, since he could not well resolve you, before ye quarter day, whether he would want any money or no, he is now gone ye progress with ye Provost, and some more of ye fellows along with him, who will scarce returne (as is supposed) this fortnight, but in his absence hath got Mr Waffe to read to me, who is extraordinary kind, and not he alone but several others of ye fellows, showes much more respect, then I can reasonablely expect which makes ye place every day more gratefull then other. This morning I received your letter and am hearty sorry yt through my ungratefulness you should be put to so much trouble, but for ye future I shall be more cautious. I return you many thanks for continuing
me Battlelar, makeing no question but I shall (through Gods assistance) in a little time, if so be you shall continue these your most acceptable kindnesses, but redeem those many years I have so obstinately squandred away. I have had my health very well. My Cosin Bar: Brougham hath got a very good place in ye South, and is gone with is wife to it. Mrs Lowther the last time I was to se her (who continues very kind) told me she had heard yt my Brother Henry was very likely to be shortly made prebend of Carlisle. I have here sent you a bill of my disbursements, and if there be any thing which you think extraordenary pray let me know of it. Pray give my love to all my Brothers and Sisters
so I rest your dutiful Son
I desire you to send to Sedbergh for these two Bookes, and let me have them by Tom: that is Aristophanes, and Godwyns Antiquities, being two bookes which I want and are not much used there.
For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal near Kendal By ye way of London.

note.value: 527. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO ROGER FLEMING.

text.p:
I have received yours of ye 10th instant, with a note of your Disbursemts therein; & I am very glad to hear that you are well; that your Tutor, Mr Waugh, & divers others of ye Fellowes, are so very kind unto you; and that you begin to like Queens College every day better than other. If you shall continue to be civil, sober, & studious, you may be assured, that good men will have a Respect for you, & that it will be for your Honor & Profit. I am very hopeful that you will make good what you promis; redeeming as much of your lost time, as you can possibly. I have sent you ten Pounds by this Bearer Tho. Burnyates. which I hope will keep you a good while from wanting. Acquaint your Tutor therewith, & that I expect from you a particular Account of wt money you shall from time to time dispense, presuming it too great a trouble for him to do it. Time & Treasure are two things that you must be a very good Husband of; and I have observed that ye hardest Students are generally ye thriftiest men. I have lately received a Letter from your Brother Michael, who is in great heart, & who likes ye Kings Camp in Flanders very well, being there well paid & haveing there all kinds of Provisions in great Plenty. The cutter of your new seal, should have
cutt therein A Rose, as a due Difference for you; being a seventh Brother. Give my service to my cosin Lowther, & my thanks to her being so obligeing unto you. I have writ unto your brother James at Sedbergh for ye 2 Books you desired, which I hope he'l send next Saturday unto Kendal, that Tho. Burnyates may convey them unto you. My service unto my Godson & Mr Waugh, with many thankes for their great care of you & kindness towards you. Remember me to all who are civil unto you. The Lord bless you, & preserve you out of all ill company. I am

note.value: 528. JAMES FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
Yours I received last Saturday, which did not answer your expectation; I have here sent you one of the Books you writ for, the other we are latly begun to read; They are to be sould here, yett their pries are very unreasonable, they are all at six shilling's; Dear Father, I was not a little surprized, when I found your commands so strictly injoyn me to that which my own Inclynations above all things disdain; Therefore, with all submission, as in Duty I am bound, I unfeignedly beg of you not that my unwillingness should cause any
displeasure, but that you would determine, and dispose of me as shortly as you see convenient, which may redound to my credit, and to your pleasure; In expectation of which, I remain
For Sr Daniel Fleming these, at Rydal.

note.value: 529. ROGER FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
Yours with ye ten pounds I received, and according to your orders, I acquainted my tutor therewith who was very well pleased, and told me I might pay all disbursements save Battles, and chamber rent, and these he would take care of. I have sent you here a bill of what I disbursed since ye tent of June, though it is more then I thought it should have been, by reason we have had ye Kings plaires here, and though I thought yt once should serve me, yet yt once was so tempting yt it got me to another, but then I resolved to do no more. My sister Bouch sent me 2s and 6d, for which I desire you to return her many thanks. I have (I thank god for it) my health very well, and likes as well, and continues pupil to my Cosin Browham, who is very kind to me. I desire you to send me with Tom: a pair or two of stokins, and Gloves, for they are very dear
here, and for socks I could not well do without them. So I rest your
For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal These.

note.value: 534. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO SIR JOHN LOWTHER OF LOWTHER.

text.p:
I hope this will find you safely arrived at London; and that your good Lady & all my Cosins are well there. My Son Henry being lately at Rose-Castle, My Lord Bishop acquainted him, that Dr Todd had writ unto his Lordship, intimating that he intended to Resign his Cure in his Lordships Diocess; which if he do, I could wish my Son Henry may be his Successor. The Doctor enjoys ye Rectory of Arthuret, situate upon ye Borders of Scotland, & valued in ye Kings Bookes at 2l~i in time of Peace, & nothing in time of War. My Lord Preston was Patron of this Liveing, which I presume now belongs to ye King, & it being of so small a value, it will belong (as some think) unto ye Lord Keeper to Present. I am altogether unknown to his Lordship, therefore I desire you to move him to present my Son, in case ye Doctor shall Resign this Rectory. I hear nothing yet concerning my Son Michael, who was in ye late Battel in Flanders. The
Lord send us good newes. My humble service unto Sr. Jo. Wentworth & all yours. I am
Sr Your most affectionate Kinsman and most obedient Servant
For Sr Jo. Lowther of Lowther These.

note.value: 536. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO SIR JOHN LOWTHER OF LOWTHER.

text.p: I am much obliged unto you for ye Favour of your last, & the Account which you were pleased to give me of Doctor Todd's writeing unto you. I hope he will not endeavour to prevail with you to forebear moveing on my son's behalfes until ye Lord Keeper shall be engaged unto some other. If his Lordship would be pleased to promis you to present my son Henry Fleming, (an Oxford Master of Arts of above 8 yeares standing) unto ye Rectory of Arthuret in Cumberland, in case ye Doctor shall Resign it, (which I presume he will ere long do, notwithstand. his pretences to ye contrary) in as much as I can desire. I have writ unto ye Doctor, but as yet I have not heard from him. I am glad to hear, that Colonel Stanley hath lately writ unto my Cosin. Tho. Preston, that my Son Michael is safe; & proves very well. All Health & Happiness is heartily wished unto yourselfe, & all yours, by Sr

note.value: 539. ROGER FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p: I have here sent you an account of ye disbursements which I have disbursed since Toms last departure, and for ye clothes mentioned in ye Bill, I am apt to think, you'l take them to be very dear, which if you do, it's as I did myself, though I could not mend my hand any where, and for ye futer (if you please) Ile have my clothes out of ye Country, for I am satisfied I may have them cheaper, for here all things are very dear, and for ye expences I hope you will not think much at, perticulerly yt of ye Treat, for I was advised to it, and I am in great hopes it will be much to my advantage. My Tutor gives his service to you, and all with you, and did not know shewerly this morning whether he would write or no, but he thought he would defer till ye quarter day which will be when Tom is here, he therefor wished me to desire you to send what money you thought convenient, for their will be three quarter daies before Tom comes up againe, he continues very kind to me. and I have my health and likes very well, which is all but my duty to you and my love to my Brothers and sisters

pray desire my sister to send me the things which I write for. My Cousin Lauther hath been so very sick yt all thought she would have died, but she's prety well recovered againe. For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal near Kendal by ye way of London.

note.value: 542. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO SIR JOHN LOWTHER OF LOWTHER.

text.p: I am infinitely obliged unto you for your speaking unto my Lord Keeper on ye behalf of my son Henry, & I hope his Lordship will remember not to dispose of ye Rectory of Arthuret without acquainting you. I have lately received a Letter from Doctor Todd, wherein are these words. I am &c. who is ye Person in ye Diocess ye Doctor means I know not; & how Lawful & Reasonable these conditions are, I referr unto your consideration. I have acquainted ye Bishop therewith; and as any thing more shall happen therein I will give you an Account thereof. God send us good Newes out of Flanders. My humble Service unto your selfe, Good Lady, and all yours. I am
Sr, Your most humble & obliged Servant

note.value: 543. JAMES FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
Yours I received with the things expressed; The britches you sent were both very fit; I returned one pare of shoo's again, being too lardge, which we received the last Saturday; our wast-coat's begins
to fail very much, and the great-coat's, which we are forc'd to wear every day uppon the other cloaths; The Master hath been very hard uppon us long, which mak's our time redound much more to our Disadvantage than anything of Profit; Dear Fater, being at ye present at a want for money, I am forced once more to trispass uppon your good Nature; a small matter would be acceptable, but much more ye sight of the Hors's; Soe with my Duty to you and my services to all my Bros and sisters, I remaine
For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal These

note.value: 545. REV. POSTHUMUS WHARTON TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
Your Son James hath put me to use all my skill, and all is too little to praevail with him to mind his business. It is (as I have frequently told him) in his power to be a proficient, to which nothing is wanting but his own care; but that alas! both has been, is, and I doubt will still be wanting, for I have tryed all the means I can, but without effect for, I hear, he declares against goeing to the Vniversity, and therefore will not at all apply himself to his study; he has of late (to my great trouble) been sometimes in the Alehouse, and induced some of his Schoolfellows to goe with him, which is a fault I could never endure in my boys, nor ever (I hope) shall, without the severest reproofs; the School has been pretty free from yt vice a long time, and I dread the thoughts of its return, and hope to use means of praevention; I desire, if you think fit, yt you'l please to try the effects
of a sharp Letter, possibly it may work something; your son ffletcher is much more willing to learn, but not soe capiable, his nature is very pleasing, but his parts slow, I will doe what lays in my power for them as I have ever done, for this is my satisfaction that my conscience bears me witness, that I have served you faithfully, though not soe effectually as I desired, and that I can in truth (as I now doe in hast) subscribe my self, Honoured Sr
This ffor the Worshipfull Sr Daniel ffleming Kt att Rydal wth care

note.value: 546. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO ROGER FLEMING.

text.p: Godwins Antiquities, which should have been sooner with you, I have now sent you, and your sister I hope hath sent you the other things you writ for. Your Letters of July 17, & of Sept. 14. last past, are come unto my hand; and I am very glad to hear of your Health, & of your likeing Oxford so well. It is your interest to study as hard, & to be as good an Husband of your money, as you can: for God knows how short a time I may live to maintain you at ye University. Avoid, as well as you can, giveing of Treats; for they seldome turne to any good Account; But A Sober, studious & civil conversation will be much more for your Advantage amongst good men. I have sent by this Bearer (Tho: Burnyate) unto your Tutor ye sum of Ten Pounds for your use, which, with what you have in your hand, will I hope serve until this Bearers next Journey. Give my service to my cosin Lowther, & I am glad to hear of her Recovery. Your brother Michael was well in ye camp in Flanders when we last heard from him & so are all your Relations in ye Country. I have writ to your Tutor, and give my service to all my good Friends in Oxon. The Lord bless you; & I wish that you dayly well discharge your Duty towards God & man. I am

note.value: 548. ROGER FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
The Booke with ye rest of things which my Sister sent me I have received, I got them weighed, and they came to four pounds and an
Half, yet I was in hopes to have received a booke or two more, particulerly Aristophanes, for we now make use of it in ye Hall, and I am very unwilling to give so much for it, as it would cost here, which makes me for ye present, trouble my Tutor for his, who is unwilling yt I should buy one, but rather send for it againe, which I have done in Jameses letter. my Tutor is extroardinary kind to me, and takes great paines with me, which makes me begin to think something of coming on ye foundation, though it will be long before I can doe it, I have so many Seniours to come on. I have here sent you a Bill of my Disbursements since ye ninth of September. Doctr Todd sent for me and gaive me a Booke, which I hope you'l return him thanks for when you write to him. Mr Nicklson of Carlisle was here lately, and sent for me two days, and made very much on me both times. This last week I had a very troublesome cold, but (I thank God) I have almost got quit of it, for several in ye University dies of it, and none with out great trouble a pain gets quit of it, for very few escapes it. I wish a merry Christmas and many of ym I am
For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal These

note.value: 550. REV. HENRY BROUGHAM TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p: I recd of Tho: Burnyeates ye ten pounds menc~on'd in your letter, and have placed it to Cous. Roger's accounts. His expences have not been great Since I Sent ye last particulars (there being only one full Quarter expired) and So his further accounts will come Soon enough, I presume sometime before ye Carrier's next return. I can only return you double thanks for yr kindness Since you are pleased to double ye ordinary allowance for Tuition; tho~ I had obligation enough before not to Suffer any care to be awanting on my part. If that, added to his own industry (wch I doubt not but he will continue) will enable us to redeem lost time; I hope we may in a good measure answer what can be expected from us, tho~ perhaps not what might be wish'd. I dare promise no further; but if you don't think of otherwise disposeing of yr Son, we shall endeavour to make ye best of it here. I am
Hond Sr Yr obedient Son & Servant
To The right Worshipfull Sr Daniel ffleming at Rydal Westmrland These.

note.value: 551. JAMES FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
Yours with a bundle I received, yett the stokins mentioned we
have heard nothing of; Last Tuesday were we sent for to Mr Trotter's, by my Bro: & Sister Tatham and my Bro: & Sister Bouch, wher we tarryed on night; Christmass being so nigh, we would have you to send for us the first day of the following moneth, for most of the Schoolers goe away at that day, yett we break not up before the 7th day; coalds has been very rife here, My Bro: Fletcher has been sore troubled with it, yett he is very well recovered. All your friends at High-Hall gave theire services to you and amongst the rest
For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal These

note.value: 552. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO SIR JOHN LOWTHER OF LOWTHER.

text.p:
I am much obliged unto you upon ye Account of my Son Henry, although he shall not reap ye benefit which you very kindly design'd him: Doctor Todd doth so delay his Resigning, as some are of opinion he hath shammed my Lord Bishop; & I hear he pretends divers
things, the reality of which may be questioned. My Son Michael is (I thank God) very hearty at Dendermond in Flanders, & hopes to be advanced, considering ye many vacancies there, and here in England. He was at great charge in Listing, Passing & Marching above 20 able Souldiers from Kendal to London; & he got no Pay for himselfe until he arrived in Flanders. He hath been an Ensign a year, he hath behaved himselfe well in ye Battel of Landen & elsewhere in Flanders, & he hopes to be preferred. If you shall be pleased to speak for him to Colonel Stanley (a member of your House) & to Mr Blaithwait, probably it may prove much to my Sons advantage. I hope my good friends will excuse me in troubling them on ye behalfe of my Sons; since I am not able to preferr them my selfe. If my Cosin Preston would speak heartily to Colonel Stanley on my son Michael's behalfe, I believe he might prevail with him. I heartily wish you, and all yours, many happy New-Yeares; & I shall ever remain
Sr Your most obliged faithful Servant
To Sr Jo. Lowther of Lowther These.

note.value: 556. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO ROGER FLEMING.

text.p:
Yours of Nov. 14. last I received by Tho. Burnyates, & I shall by him make your Tutor & you a Return. Our Carrier the next week will begin his journey towards Oxford; and I intend then to send your brother James with him. Give my service to your Tutor, & acquaint him that I hope he will be pleased to take care of James,
as well as of you, & that he'l provide for him agt his arrival at Oxford. I could wish that you two brothers might lye together, & have studies as near as may be. I doubt not, but that you will do what you can for ye welfare of you both. All your Friends here are well. My service to all with you; & the Lord bless you. I am

note.value: 559. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO ROGER FLEMING.

text.p:
I writ to you ye last week, which I hope you have received. Yours of Nov. 14 Tho. Burnyates did bring me, & by ye last post I received yours of ye 6th instant, with ye Accounts from your Tutor & your selfe. I hope you'l take what care you can of your brother James, to get him entered a Battler, as you are, to buy him a Gown, &c; & he will, I presume, be directed by you. I have sent by Tho. Burnyates 20l~i to be paid unto your Tutor & 10l~i to be paid unto you; which sums I intend for ye use of you two brothers, & in case of any want I hope your Tutor & you will helpe one another. I could wish that you Brethren (as I writ in my last) might lye together, & have studies as near as may be. I doubt not, but that your Tutor & you will take what care you can of James. He hath brought some Bookes with him, & you must supply him with such other as he shall want. Study closely, & be good Husbands, and probably Mr Provost & ye Fellowes will be kind unto you. You should let me know ye name of ye Book that Dr Todd gave you, that I may thank him for it. Let Tho. Burnyates sell James his Horse as soon, & as well as he can; Receive you the money for it & add it to your Account in which you must ever set down all your Receipts, & what remains in your hand, as well as your Disbursments. You did not in your last acquaint me with what money was then in your hand, but if ye account right you
then have Received in all 15l~i & Disbursed 9l~i - 11s - 10d. ob~. so that there will remain in your hand 5l~i - 8s - 1d. ob~, besides ye 10l~i now sent you, & James his Horse price. The more that you & James shall study, ye better it will be for you & me. The Lord bless you both. My service to all my Friends. I am

note.value: 561. JAMES FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
According to your orders, the Horse was sold shortly after my arrivement, who perform'd his journey very well, which made it much
more pleasant; I was much torment'd with the sadle, fearing it always to hurt. I had very good company, yett they caus'd my expenciss to be very high, which I hope you will pardon; Theire manner of liveing Thomas can satisfy you much better than I can express; All my sisters veer extraordanary kind to me, the morning that I came away my Sister Alice gave me 2s - 6d, at Park-House my sister Wilson 7s - 6d at Over-Hall my sister Tatham 5s at Ingleton my sister the same and at Kendal of my Cousin Browham 2s - 6d; I acquented you with my Brothers; I cannot give you an account of this place as yett; Soe with my Duty to you, I am
For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal These.

note.value: 567. REV. HENRY BROUGHAM TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p: Yr son James came safe to Oxford, but as it happens not very advantagiously for ye ffoundation; ffor there are ten or more seniors that are capable of it, And not yet admitted into it; so that he is likely to wait ye longer. He's much a better Scholar than his Brother, and I hope if he proves Industrious, may answer ye design of sending him hither; but, if I might take ye freedom to advise, there should never another Son come at that School; if you intend to breed any more up Scholars. ffor, for anything I can apprehend by them, it is in a manner left to their choice whether they will be scholars or no; and then 'tis easy to conceive what use Boys will make of that liberty, and how much it disposes them to be careless and Idle when they come hither. I must renew my thanks for ye unusual allowance you are pleased to make for Tuition, and will endeavour that nothing be awanting in me answerable to such Encouragement and ye Service and respect I have for yr ffamily.

The book wch came out under ye title of ye Genuine Remains of the late B~p of Lincolne was published by one Sr Peter Pett, a
mercenary Scribler, that has made it his busyness of late to rake into ye ashes of ye Dead. He was an acquaintance of ye Bishops, and had flatter'd him into an opinion of being his great ffriend, tho' I could never learn, either by my own knowledge whilst I lived with ye B~p; or by any enquiry I could make, that he had ever done him any Service, further than to oblige him sometimes with a letter of News or Occurrences from London. If he ever laid other Obligations upon him, I am sure he has cancell'd them all by this poor Collec~on he has published of ye B~p's Remains; wherein 'tis plain he has had no regard to ffriendship or to ye honour of ye Bishop's memory, but only to ye lucre of a few Guinys wch he had for ye Copy. ffor he has scraped together good and bad, old and new, genuine and Adulterate, only to swell ye bulk and price of ye book. A considerable part of it was printed before, and added only for ye Editor's and Bookseller's profit; as particularly the preface to ye Gunpowder treason, ye Discourse ag~st Baxter, & ye two Metaphysical Exercitations &c: wch make near a third part of ye book. only ye two former are call'd ye Substance of what ye B~p wrote, tho' ye whole is reprinted almost word for word; and for ye Exercitations they are translated out of Latin, tho' to no advantage to ye Learned, but disadvantage to ye tracts themselves. The States of Questions wch begin at page ye
568th, and in a manner conclude ye book, were such as ye Bishop wrote for com~on and Ordinary use in ye Chapell, and no more intended for ye press, than every word he spoke in com~on discourse. Besides that they are but a few of those States he left behind him, and those not judiciously chosen. The Directions to a young Divine (wch begin ye Collection) were writt 30 or 40 years agoe, and but few books (you may observe) are added since, of later date; so that it may well be presumed ye Bishop would never have suffer'd it to appear so lame and Imperfect. The Syllabus Quaestionum pag. 7 and what follows under ye title of Directions &c do's not one word of it belong to ye Authour's Copy, but is foisted in under that head, as what they thought, I suppose, some way pertinent to that Subject: tho~ the Compiler could not have pass'd a greater reflection on ye Learned Prelate's Judgmt, than to make him direct his young Divine, where to find a pestilent Heresy maintain'd to ye best advantage wth out mentioning one word of ye Authours that confute it; wch had been to prescribe poison wth out an Antidote. What was ye occasion of his writeing ye Syllabus of Socinian Questions I can give no account, if it was other, than his own private use; but 'tis certain by all his Writings and discourses, that he was a profess'd Enemy to that Sect. What remains in the Collection is such Stuff as the Editor could glean up to erect a Monument (as he pretends) to ye Bishop's memory, tho~ the materials are such, as compared wth his other Manuscripts (all wch I have by me) would make one believe him buryed in Ruines. The B~p was pleased to leave his own MSS to my Brother Chaplain & my self, but at ye same time signify'd his
pleasure not to have them printed. And ye Deference we pay to our Deceased Patron would not suffer us to violate his last Injunctions, through any prospect of advantage to our Selves. But this I can safely vouch, that if we could have been prevail'd upon to print at ye Rate that or Relique-Monger has done, it had been no hard matter to have made ye Learned Dr Barlow as Voluminous as most of ye Schoolmen. My humble Service & respects as due, in yr ffamily. I am
Hond Sr Yr obedient Son & Servt
To the Right Worshipfull Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal near Kendal Westmrld This.

note.value: 568. ROGER FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p: I suppose now it may be high time to give you an account how things goes with us, for I presume Tom will ere long be upon his journey, though this imperfect account which I am about to give will I am affrade be no little trouble to you, for this is all ye account I can send you of all ye moneys which I ought to have had in my hand, and did fear to doe it now but being fourced too it, made me, hoping yt your good nature, which allalong hath been more kind to me than either I could desire or did deserve, will be pleased to pass by this, and for ye futer, if you please I would not willingly have you to venter any more in my hand while I continue undergraduet. Pray desire my Sister to send us those Clothes which I writ for. We have our health both very well. Coll~ Grame was here ye last week and gave each of us 2s - 6d according to your orders, though James could awish'd his a little better for he cannot make it pass. Mr Brougham gives his service to you, and would have writ but he thinks he would not have occasion for anything. I believe you may have him in ye north this summer. which is all but our duty to you and love to all our Brothers and Sisters
I am your very unworthy Son
ffor Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal near Kendal By ye way of London.

note.value: 571. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO JAMES FLEMING.

text.p: I am very glad to hear that you like Oxford better & better every day; & I hope you'l make so good use of your time there, as ere long you'l be fit for Preferment. I have sent by this Bearer Tho. Burnyate 20l~i unto your Tutor, for ye use of your Brother Roger & you; & I hope by your Religious, Sober & Studious Deportment, you'l make me think my money to be very well bestowed upon you. The Lord bless you both; & let me hear sometimes from you. All here are well, & are glad to hear of your welfare. I sent you a good Halfe Crown, & although I hear you have received a bad one. Let this Bearer change it, & I will take it off his hand. So long as you shall behave your selfes well, you shall not want any thing necessary, that lies in ye power of

note.value: 572. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO REV. HENRY BROUGHAM.

text.p:
I am very much obliged unto you for ye Favour of your last kind Letter, & for your great care of, & kindness to, my sons Roger & James. I hope they continue Civil & Studious; and as they grow dayly older, so they'l improve in knowledge & vertue. I have sent you 20l~i by this Bearer, Tho. Burnyate, for ye use of my two Sons; not doubting but you'l be careful in supplying them with all necessaries, & in leaveing them with a careful Tutor, whilst you shall be out of ye College. I write this, presumeing we shall see you at ye next Assises at Carlisle. Many thanks for your exact Account of ye late Bishop
of Lincoln's Remains; which I could have wished had been otherwise published. My best service to Mr Provost, & my Cosin Lowther his sister, to Dr Mill, Dr Todd & to all ye rest of my good Friends with you in Oxon. I am
Sr, Your most obliged Kinsman & faithful Servant
For Mr Hen. Brougham at Oxon. These.

note.value: 575. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO ROGER FLEMING.

text.p:
You lost so much time at school, that if you do not use your utmost endeavours to regain it at ye University, you'l be, I fear, in great danger to be ruin'd. One of your years & experience, should be very Religious, sober, & studious; and you should not be perswaded
by any Idle, Drunken, or Debauch'd companions, to squander away your precious time or money. So long as you shall continue civil, sober & studious, I will endeavour to supply you with necessaries; otherwise you'l force me to take other measures. I do not now wonder at ye imperfect Account you gave me of your Disbursments; since they were such as you were ashamed to send me. You had better late thrive, than never. I do not love to take any more notice of your Extravagances than I am obliged to do, in order for your good. Become once more a new man, & resolve to hold to it; which will prove a comfort unto you, & to all who wish you really well. Your Tutor preached at Carlisle, & Mr Waugh at Appleby, where they came off with great honour & credit. I have not heard this long while from your brother Michael; and I wish that he may be well. All your Relations here in ye Country are, I thank God, in good health. I received your letter by Tom. B. The Lord bless you & your brother, & preserve you both out of all ill company. My Service to my Cosin Lowther, & your present Tutor. I am

note.value: 576. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO JAMES FLEMING.

text.p:
Haveing received your Letter by Tho. Burnyate, I am very glad
to hear of your likeing Queens College so well, & of your behaveing yourself so civilly, soberly, & studiously. So long as you shall be careful of avoiding all idle, Drunken, & Debauch'd companions, & so long as you shall deport your selfe according to ye Laws of God & of this Kingdom, all good men will speak well of you, it will prove for your advantage, & it will be a great comfort unto me, & all your good Friends. Make good use of your Time, now at ye University, which will make you for ever. Let no ill example prevail with you; but rather continue to be Religious, Sober, & Studious. The Lord bless you & your brother, & love one another. All your Relations here in ye Country are well. I am

note.value: 580. REV. HENRY BROUGHAM TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
If this comes time enough to yr hands, 'tis only to acquaint you that tomorrow night I design to be at Kendal, where I should be glad to see Cous: Harry or any other of yr family, if you have any further Services to Oxford, then wt you sent by Cous: George who, I hear is gone forward. When I came away, I had so much money, of yours in my hands, that ten or fifteen pounds more may serve both yr Sons till Burnyeats's next return. If Cous: George cannot furnish us, please to order by return or other wise as you have opportunity. All are well now, and so we hope this will find us all at Rydal. My ffather
& Mother sends their Services, & thanks for ye last Honour you did them.
I am Hond Sr Your obliged Son & Servant
To The right Worshipfull Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal this To be sent wth care on Tuesday night: & opened in absence.

note.value: 581. REV. GEORGE FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p: For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal These.

note.value: 583. JAMES FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p: Yors Recd the 14 of Sept: after which I hope you will pardon my boldness, having no return till the Carrier; Mr Browham arriv'd here last night with his Brother; Sr I am most asham'd to answer yors, having so bad a caracter of me; I must confess ill examples hath prevail'd too much a late; Yett I hope my deportment for the future, shall be so Religious, Sober & Studious, as shall regain your favour; Experience may teach me carefulness of avoiding all Idle, Drunken, & Debauch'd Companions; All your acquentance here are very well. All ye rest is due Respects ffrom
For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal These.

note.value: 585. ROGER FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
Yours by Tom I received, and doth here unfeignedly crave your pardon, for ye many miscaryges I have committed, not only in slighting your advice, but disobaying you commands. But I now hope, and not only yt, but fully purpose through my Brother Georges
assistance, to shake off all those fellows, which have been ye occation of those my extravigances, and for ye futer dow nothing yt either my Tutor or my Brother shall think amiss. So by these promises, (which I do realy design to perform) he upon my earnest request hath acquitted some debts, which my Brother and I had run into. Once more I desire you to forget these, and if I dow any thing hereafter which shall displease you, then leave me to my self, but yt it may not be, it shall be my whole study and care to become once more
For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal These

note.value: 589. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO REV. GEORGE FLEMING.

text.p:
I have yours by Tho. Burnyate, & I am glad to hear that you got so well to Oxford. I am much obliged to your most worthy Principal, for his very obligeing Letter, & for his great kindness unto you. Have but patience, & put your trust in God, & I doubt not all things will prove well, & to your satisfaction. I have writ to Sr Jo. Lowther, & I shall do ye like to ye rest you mention. I have sent you ye inclosed Letters unsealed for ye saveing of Postage, & that you may know what I writ. If you shall make your Function your main business, I fear not, with God's assistance, but that shortly you'l meet with Preferment. Pray be often adviseing your 2 Brothers to live Religiously, Soberly & Studiously; otherwise they will be ruined. Acquaint them Ile pay no
more Ticks for Ale, Brandy, Pipes, or Tobacco; which I abominate in any of my children. Be sure let me know truely how they behave themselves, that I may act towards them accordingly. You & my cosin Brougham will I doubt not put my money as farr as you can; & I hope that Roger & James (haveing promised me fairly) will be directed by you; it being for their Credit and profit; & for my satisfaction. You may see what I have writ unto my cosin Henry Brougham, & do accordingly, as to ye money I sent by Tom B. for you & your 2 Brothers. Your sister Tatham is brought in bed of a Daughter, who will be christened next Wednesday. My service to Mr Provost & Mr Principal, my Cosin Brougham, Mr Waugh, & to all my good Friends in Queens. The Lord bless you & your brothers. I am with thanks for your Book.

note.value: 590. REV. HENRY BROUGHAM TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
Wee fully intended to have paid our due respects at Rydal and Newhall as we return'd to Oxford; but were detain'd so long by our Friends in Cumberland, that our concerns in these parts would not admitt of any longer Stay. So that we must beg yr pardon, so we
hope my Uncle will excuse us for ye omission; not doubting but Mr High's interest will serve him for a piece of venison, when ever we are so happy as to see ye North again: at least we can well content orselves wth homelyer entertainment where we find so hearty a welcome.

Mr Waugh returns his humble Service to you, but says he did not apprehend that my L. C. Justice was desirous himself that our Sermons should be printed, but only seem'd to comply with ye motion of other gentlemen therein: and we conceive it would look more like gratifying our own ambition, than ye Publick, to catch at so slight an occasion of appearing in print; So that we had rather be excused upon that Score.

Your Sons accounts had been sent Sooner but that I waited ye Conclusion of ye Quarter on ye 21st Instant, that you might be better able to judge what Sum~e to return by next. They rise higher indeed than I expected; but in So many particulars 'tis easy to be deceived in one's guess.

I have just now recd a letter of ye Queen's desperate illness in ye Smallpox attended wth ye St Anthonies ffire. 'Tis confirmed by others both publick and private, and Some say She is already dead. I pray God it may not prove true, and avert ye ill consequences that such a disaster may forebode to the Nation. My kind respects and Services to all at Rydal, wishing them a happy new year, and that it may conclude with better news to them than 'tis usher'd in wth. I am
Hond Sr Yr most obedient Son & obliged Servant

note.value: 592. REV. HENRY BROUGHAM TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.
NO DATE

text.p: Since I recd ye 20l~i of Cous: Geo: there is another Quarter ended, wch makes ye account Swell so high. I intended to have Shewn you part of it, as far as we had gone, when in ye Countrey, but delaying it till I should see you at Rydal (as I intended) I was disappointed. However upon ye least intimation by letter I should be willing to give you what Satisfaction I can as to ye particulars. But I must own there are two things not to be justified; ye one, their battling too high; ye other, Cous: Roger's mismanagement of ye money I left wth him and what he borrowed in my name of Mr Dale one of our ffellows. What I entrusted him with was designed to discharge Several of those things wch are now sent in account: but since he failed in it, he has forfeited his credit for the future on any such Score. I have often expostulated the case with them about their batles, and will take what care I can that ye matter be mended for ye future.
To The Right Worshipfull Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal near Kendal Westmrl~d These

note.value: 593. JAMES FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
I now think it high time to write, but should have done it ere now, if my Brother had not told me he would write. I desire you to
speak to my Sister to send us our shirts and if she can our socks by Tom. I presume ere this you have received our accounts, which I can no otherwise suppose but you will think ym extraordinary, and justly you may since they realy are so, and ye reason why they are so (as I remember) I let you know in my last. One request more if you will be pleased to grant, we beg of you yt you would be so kind as to send us by Tom Three pounds, to quit some expences, which our Tutor and Brother Go: would not alow any thing for, which is all but our duty to you, and love to our Brothers and Sisters from those who have been your expensive Sons,
For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal nigh Kendal These by ye way of London

note.value: 594. REV. GEORGE FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
I received yours of ye 10th of Nov. & deliver'd the enclosed according to your directions. I have here sent you my accounts, & hope they will not displease you. I confess my Battles & Chamberrent seem to swell very high: but if, Sr, you will please to consider, yt I pay as much for my Chamber & other house dues, as if I had been resident ye whole Quarter (I having been here above half of it) you will not I suppose reckon it so unreasonable. I would before this have been Master, but yt I had not wherewith to pay the fees for it. It will
Sr cost me in the Hall above 8£. The Captain who was at Levens last Sum~er; hath express'd a great satisfaction, Sr, in ye company he had with you there; and Mr Gybson (who came this week from London,
& was last night at my Chamber) gave an account of it; he adds that Cambden will be forth within this moneth. The frost is here most severe, & additions daily of more snow so it is now very thick, and of long continuance. I wish it be not so with you; and yet for all this the Smal-Pox is here very rife & mortal. Upon Munday the Vice-Ch.
goes to Adress the K. in ye name of this Univ. Mr Waugh will this year be Proctor for Queens Col. and so my Cos. Browham is like to be disapointed of it. Sr I want Sheets & Towels, and wish I might merit so much as to deserve a Chare Pie by Tom, to help to save the Charge of treating for my degree; all are heare in mourning for the Queen. There is a Pamphlet which gives an account of the Maronites; which if you please I shall send you. here is a Book writ by Mr Lock which makes a great noise. the title is Two Treatises of Government, in ye former The false Princip. & foundations of Sr Rob. Filmer, & his Followers, are Detected & overthrown. ye latter is an Essay concerning ye true Original, Extent & End of Civil Government. Price 3s - 6d. this Lock Sr was expel'd Ch. Ch. Coll. for his
Praesb. Principals; and was Chaplain to the E. of Shaftesbury. I wish you Sr many a happy new year and Desire your Blessing; & rest
I wish Sr you could dispose of one, or both of my Brothers, for I fear they will never answer expectation where they are; they having made greater progress in Smoaking then any other thing.

note.value: 600. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO ROGER FLEMING.

text.p:
I have received your Letter of ye 20th of ye last moneth, & I perused your Tutors Accounts; and notwithstanding your promises I find you are so extravagant in your expences, as I must of necessity
order you to come hither with this Bearer Tho. Burnyate, in case your Tutor & Brother George shall judge it best for you. The Arts of Drinking & of Takeing Tobacco may be learned here in ye Country, as well as in Oxford, & at a more easy Rate. A little country Air will I hope so clear your Understanding as to make your truely sensible of your miscarriages. Be advised by your Tutor & Brother George, although you have not been by

note.value: 602. REV. HENRY BROUGHAM TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.
NO DATE

text.p:
I recd ye twenty pounds last sent by Burnyates for ye use of your two Sons, and will endeavour, what lyes in me, that it be expended according to your mind; but, when all is done, that will in
ye greatest measure depend on their management; wch I could wish had been better hitherto, and more answerable to ye desires and advice of ffriends on all hands. I fail not to second yr letters by what arguments I can; and if this will prevail, we may hope for an amendment. Upon ye mistake you mention'd in my last accounts, I im~ediately examined my book; wch I had no sooner lookt into, than I discover'd ye omission. It was, I must own, an unaccountable oversight; for I had mentioned ye Sum~e twice in my own book, both when I rec'd it, and also in sum~ing up ye accounts wch I design'd to shew you in ye North, if I had not been prevented of calling at Rydal. So that how I came to overlook it afterwards (for I assure you in ye presence of God I had no design in it) I can give no satisfactory account: only shall take warning from hence to be more circumspect hereafter in things of that nature, and must leave it to yr Candor to put a construction upon it. Cous: George brings down with him ye weight of his new degree, as deep as ye roads are: but will be expected back before or Act, to take part of ye Government upon Him. I wish his Brothers would follow so good an example of Studiousness and frugality. I leave him to tell you ye news of ye place; and shall further only add that I am
Since I wrote this Cous: George desired to have five pounds of ye twenty, finding ye expences of his Degree & Journey to rise higher than expected.
To the Worshipfull Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal near Kendal Westmrland This

note.value: 603. JAMES FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p: In yor last you were pleased to advise me from Ale and Tobacco. I have very readily obey'd yor com~ands, being still desirous (tho unable) in ye circumstances I am now in; I hope you are sensable, why ye Accounts were much otherwise then you expected; The reason of these and some other extravigances were before my Bro: Geo: arriv'd here; which he may both satisfy you with, and after what manner we liv'd since; I should have been very sorry at the news of his goeing down, if not to yor satisfaction and his profit; To desire pardon and promiss amendment, I am asham'd, haveing made it so accustamary. I cannot but acquaint you with my thoughts, and Inclynations, which I hope may prove more pleasing to you and my Future happiness; I should rather make choyce of any place, you think most convenient, than ye best Parsonage; Therefore with yor advice and assistance, I shall indeavour to settle and compose my mind to fit my self as well for ye sinceryty of my Chamber as for ye Company, and Society of my Friends, and acquaintance. So with my duty to you, I am, Sr, yor most obedient Son
For Sr Daniel Fleming att Rydal These

note.value: 605. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO REV. HENRY BROUGHAM.

text.p:
Your last, without Date, by Tho. Burnyates came (I presume not long after your writing thereof) unto my hand; & I returne you many thankes for it. I am glad that your Book has rectifyed the late
Omission; & that there is no difference between you (to whom I am so much obliged) and me, as to Any Accounts: Any man may mistake, & I as soon as any. I think our Oxford carrier will ere long be for another journey; & before he shall begin it, I shall be glad to hear how you do, & my two sons; whether they grow more civil, & studious, and be better Husbands. I will not now put them to ye charge of two letters by ye Post: But pray tell them, that I shall be very glad to hear from them, & that they have followed your good advice. I am sure it will be best for their Honour & Interest to do it. My service to Mr Provost, & all my good Friends; with my Blessing to Roger & James I am
Sr Your very affectionate Kinsman & obliged Servant

note.value: 606. JAMES FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
Neither the Interest nor Importunity of Friends extorted these few lines from me; it was the writing of soe Imprudent and Inconsidered a Letter by Tom, too much mine Enemie. Having seariously weigh'd the great disadvantag's encombent to it, I hartely beg yor pardon. I cannot but acknowledg yor perticular affection and my Obstinancy in Compliance with yor Request; I hope you will find this quarter Batles to be the best Symptom of my Reformation; But to come to a more solemne confession, it was my pollicy to make choice of such wayes as might seeme most useful for the forementioned purposes, which ere this, I hope my Bro: Geo: hath acquented you with. I can
scarcely think any one soe ignorant, not to consider his future happiness, more than the present divertment. I hope yor judgment will not passe sentence with too much rigour, but may expect ye same candor as formerly, which I can in noewise, being soe ungrateful a Son. I cannot think any way more quicker for preferment than thakeing Orders, and commendable; Soe with my prayers for your Health, I am
For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal near Kendal These By the way of London.

note.value: 607. REV. HENRY BROUGHAM TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p: I design'd to have writt 'ere ye Carrier's return (tho~ I had not rec'd yours) as well to give you an account of your sons behaviour, as to state their accounts for ye two last quarters of this year: only I waited for ye conclusion of this quarter at Midsum~er, that I might have been able to give you ye particulars in full of their expences.

Their battles, notwithstanding all that has been said, continue very high, and for my part, I can doe no more than I have already towards reforming that excess, without taking such courses as might have worse consequences. If you should again conclude from hence, that their application to their Studies has not been so great as it ought, I do not know how we can well avoid yr inference: only this I must confess, they have been more diligent of late than heretofore, and yet not so diligent as I could wish, or as their own backwardness in school-Learning do's require. Cous: James I hope may rub through
i; but truly I fear Cous: Roger will never live with any credit by his scholarship. I use this freedom, Sr, because I could never reconcile my self to ye flattering of parents into great hopes & greater expences to little purpose. Their battles this quarter that is a going on I find will not be so high as before; tho they plead some allowance ought to be made for their expences within ye College, because their expences abroad are retrenchd. But I tell them, yr allowance quarterly is sufficient, and that they have forfeited the confidence we had in them for being trusted with any more: My humble Service & respects as due. I am

note.value: 609. ROGER FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
I am afraid I have deferd writing too long, supposing yt Tom: Burn: is already on his journey, but ye reason of it was ye great expectation we had of seing my Brother ere this, for we were so inform'd by one who, not long ago, received a letter from him, and knowing yt at his arrival, I should be obliged to write, I thought, if possible, it might be as convenient to do all under one. And againe
I am satisfied, you are alredy acquinted with my business, yt is, yt you would be pleased to defray some expences which I have formerly aqcuainted you with, which would very much rejoice him who is at present
For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal near Kendal These by ye way of London

note.value: 610. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO ROGER FLEMING.

text.p: I have received your Letters of Mar. 11 last, & of ye 8th instant, & I have also received part of your Disbursements from your Tutor. I think it will be ye best both for you & me, to come into the country, where staying awhile, probably will do you no harm: therefore I would have you to come hither, upon Georges Horse, with Tom Burnyates,or sooner if you have a mind to travel another Road. Be sure have a care of your selfe & of my Horse, and leave your Bookes & other things with your Brother James (bringing down with you a particular of what you leave with him) who I hope will be careful of them. I have sent some money to your Tutor to pay of what is necessary; If three pounds will clear all your Extravagancies, I shall be willing that your Tutor do it, in hopes that as you grow Elder you will grow wiser. The Lord bless you. I am

note.value: 614. JAMES FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p: Yors of june ye 21th, I received, and according to my Bro: wch I made bold to peruse, have here sent ye particulars of what he left with me; The affects of yor last cannot easily be forgotten; How seasonable and necessary it was, I am not able to express; I am not a little troubled, when I reflect on ye gross extravagances and Irregalaryties, wch we have been guilty of late; Haveing yett some more personal ground for the Confidence of this Address; I will not desire you to take my own character for the Future; but those with whom I am intrusted, who have spent noe little time of late in advising me for the best; The love I ought to pay, obliges me particulary to yor Request; The effecting of wch is all my design, and I humbly pray that it may be look'd upon, as a Testimony of that greatest Acknowledgement wch is paid you by him, who is

After I had seald your letter, reading ye accounts over, I found nothing of that wch you ordered; wheither or no he desin's to clear it, I know not as yett, so I cannot be very well satisfy'd, pray tell me beg of you to write and desire him. For Sr Daniel Fleming These att Rydall

note.value: 616. JAMES FLEMING TO ROGER FLEMING.

text.p:
By Tom I received one from my Father, and one from my Bro: Henry, wch I made bold to peruse, yett finding nothing of any moment, I did not thinke it worth time to return them; I hope you'll excuse me; considering the great business I have had lately in hand about our extravigancies, and my own imposission, wch is not as yett finish'd, Mr Dayl has been pleased to give me a a nother, wch I have at this time, wch Mr Brougham was not well pleased with, when I
acquented him with it, he being ye occasion of my being tarde that night. The Common report here is, of yor comming noe more, wch I cannot beleive; Pray let me know if you will have yors done, and what I must doe in it. As for the ticks Mr Brougham has taken into his hand & designs to clear all of as fur as ye 10 quid will goe; soe I do not vallue one of them. I have wrot my Father ye particulars of what you left with me, as for Books, only those wch have been bought since you and I came, for ye rest you may acquent him, they are my Bro: if soe be he after send for the other things according as I have writ. As for news, Dr Swenson, Mr Dalton, and Mr Ion, came for the North ye week following, Mr. Garnet comes by
Tom; For Threlked he knows nothing of it as yett; his name is keept stopt all a long. As for ye ticke at Noes-Ark mounted to more than either you or I did think of. Several, but of what societies I know not as yett, had made bold tu use our names; I desire you to write to none of them. Characters perhaps you are scusable of; This day Mrs Minn took Barg for London, thinking it to be ye privats way, the report is of her being with child; as for ye other who excel's her as much, as wine
doth small bear, is at home ye topp of Oxon. Our bear is too strong, as several say's but I do not find it. Eastgate Ginny has got a comrade from London as bad as herr self, scarce soe pritty. Just now came I from Mr Brougham, to know what he designt to doe, who answer'd, after I had told ye tyme at Toms, he wonderd that my father would consent to any such thing, he persists more than he would have done; soe I shall acquent you with it, as soon as I know any more of it; being in hast pray excuse faults, & Lett me hear from you, when business will give you leave, with ye news of Rydall, ye next expect a more lardg account. pray keep this letter to yor selfe; Mr King buried his youngest child ye last week; soe did Heithfeild our Showmaker, his wife, who made it her business to cut her throote; Since yor absence here is one dyed who has left 3£ pound per annum for any one will take charge of his dog and its posterity.
